Infer

in-FUR -- two syllables, stress on the second syllable, FUR. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To infer to deduce something by evidence or reason.

From the empty parking lot, we could infer that the game had been canceled.

Worked Example

The teacher never announces the test. But the review sheet runs three pages, the seating chart has been redrawn, and she has asked twice whether anyone will be absent on Thursday.

From those clues a student can infer that Thursday is the test -- a conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence. Notice who does which job: the teacher's actions imply, and the student infers. The one receiving the clues is always the one who infers.

How Infer Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deduce

deduce: work something out from the evidence

conclude

conclude: decide something after reasoning it through

gather

gather: understand something from what you have seen or heard

Antonyms

guess

guess: decide with no evidence at all

misread

misread: draw the wrong conclusion from the clues

How Strong Is It? — gather → infer → deduce

gather vs. infer

gather vs. infer: Gather is the loose, everyday cousin -- 'I gather you're not coming' takes one hint and runs with it -- while infer suggests you actually weighed the evidence before deciding.

deduce vs. infer

deduce vs. infer: Deduce is the strictest of the three: you infer a likely conclusion from the clues you have, but you deduce a conclusion the evidence forces on you -- the detective's word, not the guesser's.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: in, into (Latin)

root — fer-

root — fer-: to carry, to bring (Latin ferre)

Put it together

Put it together: Infer comes from Latin inferre -- in- ('in') plus ferre ('to carry') -- 'to carry in.' When you infer, you carry a conclusion INTO your own mind from the evidence in front of you. That direction is the whole difference from imply, where a speaker sends a hint out.

Use the root in a new word: transfer

Use the root in a new word: transfer: She had to transfer her notes from the whiteboard to her notebook before class ended.

Root Check

Word Choice

One rule matters most: the listener or reader INFERS; the speaker or writer IMPLIES. If a coach says 'some of you did not run today,' he is implying that some players slacked off, and the players infer it. Never write 'his tone inferred anger' -- a tone cannot infer, because inferring is something a mind does with evidence.
